title: Conejos Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Conejos wells have a 64 ft median depth, 13 gpm median yield, and typical completed costs of $9,200-$16,800.
h1: Conejos, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land or a home near Conejos means looking past the presence of a well and checking its actual construction record. Within 5 miles of Conejos, Colorado DWR records show 1,004 permitted wells. Of those, 733 are recorded as constructed, 727 report total depth, 140 report pump yield, and 68 report static water level.

The local record is generally favorable on production: the median reported yield is 13.0 gallons per minute, while the median completed depth is 64 feet. Those figures are useful for planning, but they are not a guarantee for an individual lot. Ground conditions, well location, casing, pump equipment, and the quality of the original test all matter.

sections.heading: Conejos well depths are usually shallow, but not always
sections.html:
The median well depth around Conejos is 64 feet. The middle half of reported wells falls from 40 to 120 feet, which gives a driller a practical starting range for estimating a typical hole. Sixty-five percent of the reported wells are under 100 feet, and 28% fall between 100 and 300 feet.

Depth still varies sharply across the area. Six percent are between 300 and 600 feet, 1% are deeper than 600 feet, and the deepest record reaches 787 feet. Permits identify the unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer for 948 wells, with additional wells in the Unconfined San Luis Vall and Unconfined San Luis Valley aquifers. A bid should account for the actual parcel, access, casing, grout, and the possibility that fractured rock will not behave like a nearby well.

sections.heading: Reported Conejos yields are strong, with limited testing records
sections.html:
Only 140 wells in the records report a pump yield, so the yield statistics do not describe every permitted well. Among reported results, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-six percent report more than 15 gallons per minute, while 53% fall from 5 to 15 gallons per minute.

One percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and none of the reported wells are under 1 gallon per minute. For a buyer, that reduces concern about extremely poor production in the recorded sample, but it does not replace a current flow test. Confirm the well’s permitted use, pump performance, storage capacity, and recovery before assuming it will support a house, stock, irrigation, or future construction.

sections.heading: Water levels near Conejos have stayed broadly similar
sections.html:
Reported static water levels have a median depth of 51 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 30 to 132 feet. That spread matters when planning a pump: a property with water at 30 feet presents a different equipment and service condition from one near the deeper end of the local range.

The decade comparison does not show a clear dropping trend in these records. The median measured depth to water was 51 feet in the 2010s and 48 feet in the 2020s, meaning the later median was slightly shallower. Only 68 wells report a static water level, so treat this as a record summary rather than a parcel-specific forecast. A driller or pump contractor should measure the subject well and check neighboring wells near Antonito and Romeo when evaluating a property.

sections.heading: Permit history shows steady drilling through the Conejos area
sections.html:
Permit activity extends back to the 1950s, when 13 permits were issued. The record rises to 140 in the 1970s, 97 in the 1980s, 112 in the 1990s, and 210 in the 2000s. There were 131 permits in the 2010s and 68 in the 2020s, with the newest permit year listed as 2025.

Most recorded use is domestic or household at 78%. Stock use appears on 38% of permits, irrigation on 5%, and monitoring on 3%. The most active drillers in these records are Heersink Drilling, also listed as Heersink, Scott, with 98 wells; Valley Pump Company, listed as Self, Clinton L., with 83; and Larry Burk Drilling, listed as Burk, Larry, with 47. Verify licensing, scope, and current references before hiring.

sections.heading: A median-depth Conejos well pencils out at a defined range
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At a typical drilling rate of $50 to $75 per foot, drilling to the 64-foot median depth works out to about $3,200 to $4,800 for the drilled hole. That is not the full project cost.

A finished well, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, is estimated at $9,200 to $16,800 at the median depth. A deeper hole, difficult access, additional casing or grout, longer utility runs, and challenging subsurface conditions can push the price higher. Ask each bidder to separate drilling, casing, development, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, and testing. Comparing only the per-foot rate can leave major parts of the installation outside the quote.

sections.heading: Check water quality, septic space, and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
There is 1 mapped PFAS sampling or contamination site and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site within about 10 miles of Conejos. No historic mine features are mapped in that search area. These records do not establish that a particular well is contaminated or clean. Test the well water through a qualified laboratory, especially before relying on it for household use.

Low yield and dry holes remain site risks even with a favorable local median. Review the permit, completion report, construction details, pump test, and maintenance history. On a building lot, confirm that the well location, septic system, replacement area, driveway, and house site can coexist with required separation and access. A DWR permit and an existing well are not the same as a guarantee that the property can support every proposed use.

sections.heading: Do the parcel-level checks before buying near Conejos
sections.html:
Start with the Colorado DWR permit and construction records for the exact well. Confirm the permitted use, depth, aquifer description, static water level, yield test, pump equipment, and whether the records identify the well as constructed. If the property is vacant, have a driller review nearby completions before setting a budget.

For a new well, get a written proposal that addresses access, the expected depth range, casing and grout, well development, pump sizing, storage, trenching, electrical work, and testing. Household-use wells are commonly regulated as exempt wells, but the permit controls the allowed use and the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit applies to exempt wells. If a proposed use involves an over-appropriated basin, ask whether an augmentation plan is required. Compare Conejos with nearby Antonito, Manassa, and La Jara records, but do not treat distance alone as proof of matching conditions.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Conejos, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Conejos is 64 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 120 feet, and 65% of reported wells are under 100 feet. Depth is not uniform: the deepest record reaches 787 feet. A driller should review the exact parcel and nearby completion records before giving a firm depth estimate.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Conejos?
faq.a: The local cost model uses $50 to $75 per foot in mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground. At the 64-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $3,200 to $4,800. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical work is estimated at $9,200 to $16,800. Difficult access or greater depth can increase the total.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Conejos?
faq.a: Among the 140 wells with reported pump yields, the median is 13.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 10.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Forty-six percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Because most permitted wells do not report a yield, buyers should obtain a current flow or pump test for the specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Conejos?
faq.a: The well records do not prove that any individual water supply is safe or unsafe. One PFAS sampling or contamination site and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site are mapped within about 10 miles. Test the property’s water through a qualified laboratory before drinking it, and review the well construction, location, and septic arrangement.

faq.q: Are Conejos wells getting deeper or losing water?
faq.a: The available static-water records do not show a clear decline. The median depth to water was 51 feet below the surface in the 2010s and 48 feet in the 2020s. Only 68 wells report static water levels, so this comparison is limited. Measure the subject well and review nearby records rather than relying on the countywide summary.
